literal: As Zhou troops came to raid, Chancellor Gao Anaigong led troops to the relief; Yong's allocations and distributions were not fully approved, and on this account a rift opened.
idiomatic: When Zhou troops came to raid, Chancellor Gao Anaigong led an army to relieve the siege; Tang Yong's supply allotments were not fully approved, and the two fell out.

literal: Anaigong slandered him and sent Attendant-in-Ordinary Hulu Xiaoxiaoqing to proclaim an edict rebuking and reproaching him; Yong was detained in custody and soon released.
idiomatic: Anaigong slandered him and sent Attendant-in-Ordinary Hulu Xiaoxiaoqing with an edict of rebuke; Tang Yong was held in custody, then soon released.

literal: As the imperial carriage was about to visit Jinyang, an edict ordered Xiaoxiaoqing to take overall charge of cavalry expenditures; he decided most matters on his own and did not consult or report upward.
idiomatic: As the emperor was about to visit Jinyang, an edict put Hulu Xiaoxiaoqing in overall charge of cavalry expenditures; he decided most matters himself and did not consult or report upward.

literal: Yong relied on himself—from the hegemonic court onward he had constantly held pivotal posts, served six emperors, and received very heavy favor—yet was suddenly slighted by Xiaoxiaoqing; resentful and sullen, he showed it in word and countenance.
idiomatic: Tang Yong relied on having held pivotal posts since the hegemonic court, served six emperors, and enjoyed heavy favor—yet was suddenly slighted by Xiaoxiaoqing; bitter and sullen, he showed it in speech and face.

literal: After the emperor's defeat at Pingyang, he returned to the capital Ye in disarray.
idiomatic: After the emperor's defeat at Pingyang, he fled back to Ye in disarray.

literal: Yong feared Anaigong would slander him again and hated that Hulu Xiaoxiaoqing slighted him; he therefore remained at Jinyang and, with Moduolou Jingxian and others, elevated the Prince of Ande as emperor.
idiomatic: Tang Yong feared Anaigong would slander him again and resented Hulu Xiaoxiaoqing's slight; he stayed at Jinyang and, with Moduolou Jingxian and others, elevated the Prince of Ande as emperor.

literal: Within a day or two the city fell; Yong then surrendered to Zhou and was appointed, by precedent, Pillar of State and Grand General.
idiomatic: Within a day or two the city fell; Tang Yong surrendered to Zhou and, by precedent, was made Pillar of State and grand general.

literal: He died while serving as governor of Feng Province.
idiomatic: He died as governor of Feng Province.

literal: Yong was by nature intelligent and keen, understood current affairs, and throughout the Northern Qi line held command of military affairs.
idiomatic: Tang Yong was intelligent and keen by nature, understood current affairs, and throughout Northern Qi held command of military affairs.

literal: All troops of the nine provinces, valiant recruits from the four quarters, their strength and numbers, rotations coming and going, and the fineness of weapons and fullness or emptiness of grain stores—he worked at these with keen care and knew them all thoroughly.
idiomatic: Troops of the nine provinces, valiant recruits from the four quarters, their strength and numbers, rotations, the quality of weapons, and the state of grain stores—he tracked all of it with keen care and knew it thoroughly.

literal: From the Daning era onward luxury and waste ran rampant; by the end of Wuping the treasury stores were gradually depleted.
idiomatic: From the Daning era on, luxury and waste ran rampant; by the end of Wuping the treasury was gradually empty.

literal: Yong's revenue decisions in expenditure brought great benefit.
idiomatic: Tang Yong's revenue and expenditure decisions brought great benefit.

literal: Yet once favored in appointment his spirit grew gradually haughty; many cases in which he had not lodged petitions through the departmental offices but reviewed memorials on his own authority were impeached by the Censorate and the left vice-director—all were pardoned by imperial annotation.
idiomatic: Yet once in favor his pride grew; many times he reviewed memorials without going through the offices, and the Censorate and left vice-director impeached him—all were pardoned by imperial note.

literal: Attendant of the Ministry of Works Feng Changye and secretary of the Grand Commandant's office Ping Tao both exceeded the limit on recruitment money; Yong had each beaten on the back twenty strokes.
idiomatic: Feng Changye, attendant of the Ministry of Works, and Ping Tao, secretary in the Grand Commandant's office, both exceeded the recruitment-money limit; Tang Yong had each flogged on the back twenty strokes.

literal: In Qi times no chancellor had yet beaten or flogged court gentlemen; at this the court was greatly shocked.
idiomatic: In Qi no chancellor had yet beaten a court gentleman; this greatly shocked public opinion.

literal: Yong had three sons.
idiomatic: Tang Yong had three sons.

literal: His eldest son Junming held the rank Opening Ritual, Equal to the Three Dukes.
idiomatic: His eldest son Junming held the rank opening ritual, equal to the three dukes.

literal: At the beginning of Sui's Kaihuang era he died as governor of Ying Province.
idiomatic: At the beginning of Sui's Kaihuang era he died as governor of Ying Province.

literal: His second son Junche was secretariat gentleman; he served as governor of the two Sui provinces Shun and Rong; in the Daye era he died as martial guard commandant.
idiomatic: His second son Junche was a secretariat gentleman and governor of Shun and Rong under Sui; in the Daye era he died as martial guard commandant.

literal: His youngest son Junde was executed by law because Yong had surrendered to Zhou.
idiomatic: His youngest son Junde was executed because Tang Yong had surrendered to Zhou.

literal: In Northern Qi, because the Grand Ancestor was made chancellor, the Grand Chancellor's office external military bureau and cavalry bureau divided control of troops and horses.
idiomatic: In Northern Qi, when the Grand Ancestor became chancellor, the grand chancellor's external military bureau and cavalry bureau divided control of troops and horses.

literal: When Tianbao received the mandate, all office supervisors were folded into the Masters of Writing, but these two bureaus were not abolished; Tang Yong and Bai Jian were put in charge of them, called the External Troops Department and Cavalry Department.
idiomatic: When Tianbao received the mandate, all office supervisors went to the Masters of Writing, but these two bureaus remained; Tang Yong and Bai Jian headed them, called the External Troops Department and Cavalry Department.

literal: Later Yong and Jian's standing grew ever loftier; each became head of his department; secretariat gentlemen were assigned to divide decisions on the two departments' affairs—hence the age called them Tang and Bai.
idiomatic: Later Yong and Jian rose higher; each became head of his department, with secretariat gentlemen to divide their affairs—hence the age called them Tang and Bai.

literal: Bai Jian, styled Yansu, was a native of Yangyi in Taiyuan.
idiomatic: Bai Jian, styled Yansu, was from Yangyi in Taiyuan.

literal: He first entered the Grand Chancellor's office cavalry bureau, kept charge of clerical registers, understood bookkeeping clearly, and was pushed forward by colleagues in the same office.
idiomatic: He first entered the grand chancellor's cavalry bureau, kept the clerical registers, understood accounts, and was promoted by colleagues in the same office.

literal: In the tenth year of Tianbao he was additionally made secretariat gentleman.
idiomatic: In the tenth year of Tianbao he was additionally made secretariat gentleman.

literal: When Suzong was regent he was appointed grand chancellor's office cavalry adjutant.
idiomatic: When Suzong was regent he was appointed cavalry adjutant in the grand chancellor's office.

literal: In the third year of Heqing, when the Turks invaded the border, the Dai and Xin herds were all fine horses, numbering tens of thousands together; they sheltered from bandits in Cypress Valley north of Mount Wutai.
idiomatic: In the third year of Heqing, when Turks raided the border, the Dai and Xin herds—all fine horses, tens of thousands together—hid from bandits in Cypress Valley north of Mount Wutai.

literal: After the bandits retreated, an edict ordered Jian to go there and inspect; messengers were continually sent to Jian to take over the horses and deliver them to Ding Province to be given to the people for raising and feeding.
idiomatic: After the raiders withdrew, an edict sent Jian to inspect; messengers kept coming for him to take the horses and send them to Ding Province for the people to raise.

literal: Jian judged that the horses had long gone without food and were emaciated; sending them far he feared many would die in transit; he therefore disobeyed the edict and acted on expedient grounds, dispersing and entrusting them nearby to soldiers.
idiomatic: Jian judged the horses had long gone unfed and were thin; a long haul would kill many, so he disobeyed the edict, acted as expedient required, and distributed them nearby to soldiers.

literal: He reported and the emperor learned; an edict permitted it.
idiomatic: He reported; the emperor learned and approved by edict.

literal: The war horses suffered no loss—Jian had merit in this.
idiomatic: The war horses suffered no loss—Jian had credit for this.

literal: At the end of Wuping he rose through special advance, attendant-in-ordinary, and chief minister of the secretariat.
idiomatic: At the end of Wuping he rose through special advance, attendant-in-ordinary, and chief minister of the secretariat.

literal: Jian had no other talent but was diligent in public duty.
idiomatic: Jian had no other talent but was diligent in public affairs.

literal: As the royal enterprise was just beginning and military trust was weighty, Jian and Tang Yong both rose to minister and chancellor by keeping charge of troops and horses.
idiomatic: As the royal enterprise was just beginning and military trust was weighty, Jian and Tang Yong both reached minister and chancellor by holding charge of troops and horses.

literal: Jinyang was the realm's lower capital; each year the emperor visited it; levies and corvée were dispatched, responsibility fixed on the provinces and commanderies.
idiomatic: Jinyang was the realm's lower capital; each year the emperor visited, and levies and corvée fell on the provinces and commanderies.

literal: Retainers and administrators of his original domain, and even district magistrates, came to consult and present requests—they had no leisure to rest.
idiomatic: Retainers and magistrates of his original domain came to consult and petition—they had no rest.

literal: Though his sons were still young, all became chief clerks in the provinces and commanderies; when the new ruler chose and appointed, they were always summoned and engaged first.
idiomatic: Though his sons were still young, all became provincial chief clerks; when the new ruler made appointments, they were always summoned first.

literal: When sons married and daughters wed, they all won eminent company.
idiomatic: Sons' marriages and daughters' weddings all matched leading families.

literal: The age regarded this as the summit of honor and favor.
idiomatic: The age took this as the height of honor and favor.

literal: In the seventh year of Wuping he died.
idiomatic: In the seventh year of Wuping he died.

literal: The full text uses the Zhonghua Shuju first edition of the Book of Northern Qi (November 1972) as the base for collation.
idiomatic: The full text uses the Zhonghua Shuju first edition of the Book of Northern Qi (November 1972) as the base for collation.
